<reason>A opened with four distinct harm lines (accountability gap, distinction/proportionality brittleness, flash-crash escalation risk, cheap proliferation) and then used B's own chosen examples (landmines, cluster munitions) as evidence for the accountability-fiction claim, a sharp and original turn. Critically, B never substantively engaged the escalation/flash-crash argument at all, and only lightly touched the ML-brittleness point, leaving two of A's four main pillars largely standing through the whole debate. Both sides executed the Pressure Questions and A1/A2 format correctly, which is a wash. B's strongest sustained line — verification is impossible because it polices an absence — was well argued and forced A to work, but A's answer that B's own proposed "restraint" (mandatory human review of context before engagement) is functionally identical to "meaningful human control" was a clever and largely successful reframe, showing convergence on substance while B was left arguing about packaging. B's closing rebuttal (positive vs. negative verification, Phalanx carve-out undrafted) was a genuine and well-organized comeback and kept the debate competitive, but it didn't recover the two entirely dropped harm lines or fully dislodge the convergence point. On balance A built the broader, more resilient case and better exploited the exchanges.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 move turning B's own landmines/cluster-munitions examples into proof of the accountability-fiction, combined with A's closing observation that B's own proposed "restraint" in Rebuttal 2 (mandatory human review before engagement) is definitionally the same as "meaningful human control" — forcing B to fight over labels rather than substance.</best_rebuttal>
